Text:
Abstract: In the world of interconnected devices also referred to as the Internet of Things (IoT) in the modern 
era, it’s important to ensure that computing resources are allocated efficiently to nearby devices such as edge, fog, 
or cloud systems to meet resource needs. However, problems such as delays in data transmission, high energy 
consumption, and slow response times can negatively impact the performance of time-sensitive applications in 
cloud-based environments.  
This paper presents the Context-Aware Offloading Framework (CAOF) for resource-constrained IoT 
applications. CAOF leverages contextual information to identify scenarios where offloading tasks to the cloud or 
to the local instances are beneficial. The framework aims to make optimal offloading decisions to improve system 
performance and minimize energy consumption. The effectiveness of CAOF is evaluated through simulations, 
comparing its performance against established offloading frameworks. CAOF is implemented as a middleware 
solution within an Amazon Web Services (AWS) ecosystem. This middleware integrates a Greengrass intelligent 
gateway that dynamically determines how to handle incoming data based on contextual information. The 
intelligent gateway can either process the data on local Elastic Cloud Compute (EC2) instances, effectively 
creating a fog layer, or send it directly to the cloud for further processing. 
Experimental results demonstrate that CAOF achieves an energy consumption of 0.0011 joules approximately, 
with an memory utilization of 3.46 MB calculated as and average over all the EC2 machines. The framework 
execution time, averaging 4.07 seconds on edge, 5.41 seconds on cloud, and only 0.56 seconds when leveraging 
EC2 instances specifically, including an 80.4% accuracy in multi-class classification tasks. The CAOF 
systematically selects the most suitable alternatives for each offloading scenario to optimize efficiency in terms 
of time, memory, CPU, and energy consumption. The proposed smart gateway framework utilizes a hybrid 
approach to make optimal offloading decisions by considering contextual data. The research concludes with the 
design and development of an edge or fog-based framework that uses smart computing to make decisions using 
machine learning reasoning. The proposed framework architecture incorporates feature selection, classification, 
and hybrid logistic regression-based learning for the most effective offloading solution.

1. Introduction 
 
Internet of Things (IoT)-based applications and services have grown as essential to many aspects of 
contemporary life, including smart cities, smart homes, industrial operations, and agriculture. Data quantities have 
increased significantly as a result of IoT expansion, mostly from sensors included in endpoint devices [1]. Due to 
its sheer volume, local processing of such large and complex sensor data has become unfeasible. The ever-growing 
volume and complexity of sensor data generated by IoT devices demand fast processing and computation. Critical 
applications and services rely on real-time data analysis while minimizing energy consumption. To address these 
challenges, designing and implementing a compute offloading architecture is essential. This approach is 
particularly crucial in the context of the Internet of Things (IoT), where diverse applications and services generate 
significant processing loads that require efficient resource management to meet strict performance requirements 
[2]. 
Computation offloading, a technique that minimizes device energy consumption and processing times, emerges 
as a potential solution for resource-constrained IoT applications. However, a key challenge lies in identifying 
scenarios where offloading tasks to a more powerful resource, like the cloud, is truly beneficial [3]. The ability to 
discern when offloading computation and data is suitable, and to learn from the context of incoming data, presents 
a significant hurdle. To address this challenge and make optimal offloading decisions, developing a context-aware 
offloading framework is crucial for computationally demanding IoT applications.

1.2 Offloading Solutions as Objective Using Edge/Fog Computing 
 
While advancements in network technology have improved capabilities, they haven't entirely eliminated 
limitations regarding energy and time efficiency. Cloud-based processing faces limitations due to physical 
distance, introducing latency. Conversely, edge nodes, while geographically closer to data sources, often possess 
limited processing power compared to centralized data centers. These factors highlight the need for intelligent 
offloading strategies that consider both resource availability and the specific characteristics of the data. 
The limitations of cloud computing for resource-constrained IoT applications, particularly regarding service 
delivery latency and processing power, can be addressed by integrating Fog and Edge Computing (FC) with cloud 
technologies [1]. In scenarios requiring significant processing capabilities, client devices rely on remote resources 
to handle and execute tasks, receiving the results afterward [2]. This approach, known as offloading, essentially 
outsources computational tasks to server-side resources. 
In this framework, the middleware layer is tasked with processing and storing data and plays a critical part in 
enabling context-aware and time-sensitive services for IoT applications through computation offloading. Edge/fog 
servers act as intelligent gateways, capable of storing data and performing operations locally, unlike the traditional 
model of relying solely on cloud servers for processing and storage. This strategy aims to improve various 
performance metrics, ultimately reducing energy consumption and latency in services delivered to IoT devices 
and applications, ensuring timely and intelligent service delivery for end users. 
Even though 5G networks and technologies are being used, it is hard for delay-sensitive apps and cloud services 
to work together because key performance metrics like latency, energy use, bandwidth, and reaction time exceed 
threshold levels [3]. The middleware layer in the IoT design looks to serve as a good solution to deal with these 
problems and meet the stringent requirements for high-task offloading. The use of Fog Computing (FC) in the 
middleware layer is supported by ongoing research because it effectively meets the needs of delay-sensitive apps 
and connects edge and cloud services. But FC has some problems, mainly because Fog nodes don't have enough 
resources, especially for jobs requiring high computing power. It is important to remember that fog computing 
works best when combined with cloud services, not when used instead. The proposed framework includes a 
combined answer that uses cloud and fog computing together in a way that works better than either one alone. 
Both act as equivalents and provide services following task requirements, but FC is relatively closer to the 
devices than a cloud architecture for computing. There also exists an issue when a decision is to be made about 
what should be offloaded: data, computation, or application, and more particularly, where to offload: fog or cloud, 
and how much to offload. The proposed offloading framework will work as a solution to such problems and will 
enable an effective and accurate decision regarding offloading. Regarding task-related variables like task size, 
duration, arrival rate, and required resources, a collaboration between fog and clouds is random. Dynamic task 
offloading is essential for maximizing the resources available in the fog and cloud to improve Quality of Service 
(QoS). Since the task's establishment, the problem of the offloading procedure is a bit complex, so the present 
work addresses it and presents an intelligent task-based framework for offloading. 
 
1.3 Contribution of the Presented Work 
 
A unique approach has been introduced to tackle the challenges faced by the Internet of Things (IoT) architecture. 
This approach involves incorporating Fog Computing (FC) into the middleware layer. This leads to an improved 
cloud structure that contains edge services. These edge services are capable of effectively implementing time-
sensitive applications. It is important to note that Fog Computing is not intended to replace cloud technology. 
Rather, it serves as an additional extension that combines the benefits of both paradigms.  
The proposed framework efficiently manages offloading by leveraging cloud and fog computing to make 
intelligent decisions. The implemented solution, called Context-Aware Offloading Framework (CAOF), utilizes 
machine learning reasoning to optimize job offloading within fog-based cloud systems. The architecture 
incorporates feature selection, classification, and hybrid logistic regression-based learning within the CAOF 
framework to deliver an effective offloading solution.

2. Background Study & Literature Review 
 
The literature study starts by discussing the importance of context and its crucial role in the Internet of Things 
(IoT). It explores how understanding context can be used to reduce workload and enhance decision-making skills. 
The research paper also delves into the use of machine learning and deep learning methods to identify contextual 
cues and improve the decision-making process. To achieve this, the study systematically and comprehensively 
reviews current literature, focusing specifically on evaluating and comparing different models and offloading 
frameworks. 
2.1 Background Study for Offloading with Context Identification 
 
Recognizing the context in which an application is being used is a crucial aspect of determining when and where 
to offload tasks. This is known as context identification and involves analyzing and interpreting the behaviour of 
the application, as well as investigating its service requirements, to gain a comprehensive understanding of the 
context or to assess the sensitivity of the application. According to Abowd et al. [4], context can be defined as 
"the information that can be used to describe the condition of an entity".  
To determine the underlying causes of the development or existence of a specific scenario, this process 
seeks to understand who, when, and what entities are involved in the situations [5]. Sensing must be the main 
priority while developing a context-aware computing framework in order to analyse incoming data and enable 
continuous learning. This need results from the enormous amount and continual nature of data produced by 
physical objects and sensors, which makes learning and making inference difficult. Neural and deep learning 
methods, along with other big data and machine learning techniques, have been used to address these issues [6]. 
An emotional computing paradigm that combines context-aware systems to identify learning inferences from 
context data is presented by Nalepa et al. [7]. although deep and neural learning can lead to excessive utilization 
of time.  
In an effort to create high-level conceptual models, researchers have focused their efforts on creating 
computationally ubiquitous frameworks [8–9]. However, given the current situation, the middleware system 
architecture faces scaling challenges. Although middleware can gather data, process information, and recognise 
context [10], its lack of services and readily available resources presents difficulties [9, 10]. Given that energy 
efficiency in context-aware applications is difficult to achieve due in large part to continuous extraction and 
inference learning from sensing devices, middleware architecture that promotes context awareness between 
application development tasks and tackles resource and service scarcity concerns is essential.

2.4 IoT Offloading Frameworks 
Existing research explores various approaches to implement offloading frameworks. These approaches include: 
• 
Application Partitioning: Dividing applications into smaller modules based on functionality. Specific 
modules requiring more processing power can be targeted for offloading [21, 22, 23]. 
• 
Thread Migration: Moving individual threads within an application to a more powerful resource for 
execution, potentially the cloud [24, 25]. 


• 
Server-Side Application Migration: Transferring the entire application to a server-side environment 
for processing [24, 25]. 
Several factors influence the decision to offload and the target location. These factors can be broadly categorized 
as internal (application needs, device capabilities) and external (network conditions) [26, 27]. 
Edge/fog computing can help cloud computing provide delay-sensitive and context-aware services in the 
Internet of Things (IoT) era by transferring data computation and service provision to the edge/fog. Fog computing 
leverages local processing power and nearby devices' capabilities (often called fog nodes) to deliver real-time and 
intelligent services for IoT applications. However, several challenges need to be addressed to fully realize the 
potential of edge/fog computing. Firstly, efficient data storage and computing management, optimizing the 
distribution and management of data storage and computation across fog nodes is crucial for efficient resource 
utilization. Second, seamless fog-cloud collaboration where establishing effective communication and 
collaboration between fog servers and cloud servers is essential for achieving scalability and handling diverse 
workloads. Third in terms of security and privacy considerations, where robust security mechanisms and privacy-
preserving techniques are needed to protect sensitive data and ensure system integrity within the fog computing 
environment. Offloading frameworks and models vary depending on the chosen offloading strategy (edge, fog, or 
cloud) and the specific optimization parameters (e.g., energy consumption, processing time, battery usage). 
An offloading framework is MAUI, which focuses on offloading tasks to smartphones to extend their battery 
life [21]. This framework partitions program code, analyzes its performance characteristics and formulates and 
solves optimization problems to achieve energy savings. Additionally, MAUI simplifies the process of 
migrating smartphone applications to the cloud. 
Kosta et al. (2012) [28] proposed ThinkAir, a framework that simplifies smartphone app migration to the cloud. 
ThinkAir uses cloud smartphone virtualization to offload method-level computing. It parallelizes method 
execution utilizing numerous Virtual Machine (VM) images to maximize mobile cloud computing's elasticity and 
scalability. ThinkAir is tested using micro-benchmarks to complex applications. It reduces execution time and 
energy usage by two orders of magnitude for an N-queens puzzle game and one order for face detection and virus 
check applications. 
A mobile cloud offloading system decision engine decides whether to offload a method to cloud servers. The 
authors construct and analyse a Context-Aware Decision Algorithm (CADA) to optimize mobile device 
performance for response time and energy usage. CADA works with many mobile cloud offloading technologies. 
The CADA algorithm was merged with ThinkAir by Lin et al. (2013) [29] to decide whether to offload a technique 
to cloud servers. 
MobiByte is a context-based progressive application model for mobile cloud computing. Multiple data 
offloading solutions improve mobile programme performance, energy efficiency, and execution support [30]. 
The cloud-based Evidence-Aware Mobile Computational Offloading (EMCO) tools and platform [12] solve 
computational offloading problems. Dedicated computer infrastructure offloads computationally heavy activities 
to surrogate clouds. Crowd sensed evidence traces categorize ambient elements and other offloading choice 
criteria. Models are built in the cloud and transmitted to mobile devices, eliminating data processing. 
Context-Sensitive Offloading System Model [31] (CoSMOS) presents a context-aware technique for Mobile 
Cloud Computing (MCC) systems, which is a self-adaptive offloading system. A decision-taking estimation-based 
approach improves application assessment of the execution time and power usage of an application. 
MobiCOP-IoT [32] deploys surrogates on far-end clouds and proximate nodes.  Edge-based nodes can 
automatically offload arbitrary tasks based on an integrated decision-making engine. MobiCOP-IoT has many 
functions, but it needs human configuration to select whether to use cloud or edge mode. MobiCOP-IoT's decision-
making engine does not consider framework energy usage, thus server IP must be specified manually. 
Mobile fog settings use a computation-offloading edge/fog mobile-based Autonomic Management Framework 
[33]. Fog nodes offer parallelism, and a code analyzer unit identifies computation-hungry blocks. Resource 
availability and network state determine latency and resource consumption. 
Several studies explore machine learning approaches for context-aware offloading decisions in IoT 
environments. One such work by [34] proposes a Context-Sensitive Offloading System (CSOS) that uses machine 
learning to determine optimal offloading scenarios. The study evaluated several algorithms, including J48, JRIP, 
IBK, and Naive Bayes. Ultimately, J48 and JRIP were chosen due to their effectiveness in identifying the best 
offloading conditions. Notably, the CSOS system emphasizes processing contextual data and transforming it into 
a high-level representation suitable for machine learning-based decision making. CSOS follows the client-server 
concept and uses history-based prediction to forecast future performance. 
The FC-based analytical model is suggested for IoT-based healthcare applications [35], the latency-critical 


nature of these services necessitates rapid processing. The architecture of cloud-based servers alone cannot meet 
the service-time requirements of such applications. For IoT data transmission, overall communication latency 
must be reduced, along with computation and network latency. As a proposed solution, an edge-based structure 
is proposed, where edges are used for data processing and analysis to reduce high latency. 
Mobile Devices (MDs) transfer resource-intensive operations to a nearby Mobile Edge Server (MES) for 
execution in order to reduce energy usage and service latency. However, the offloading choice made by MDs may 
not result in the lowest cost due to time-varying network conditions and also limited computing resources at MES. 
To reduce the overall cost of MDs, Authors [36] provide an Energy efficient and Faster Deep learning based 
Offloading Technique (EFDOT) in this work. 
Bukhari, M.M. et al., 2022[3] proposed a middleware approach for offloading that can handle delay-sensitive 
applications at the network edge. Fog computing is closer to devices than cloud computing, yet both provide task-
specific services. Fog-cloud cooperation is stochastic for task size, duration, arrival rate, and resources. Dynamic 
task offloading improves QoS by better using fog and cloud resources. The study article discusses the intricacy of 
work offloading policy design and proposes an intelligent approach. Simulations illustrate the logistic regression 
model's validity, reaching 86% accuracy compared to other algorithms, and trust in the policy of offloading 
predictive duties by maintaining process consistency and dependability. 
This research presents a unique, effective Data-Size Aware Offloading Model (DSAOM) to predict the

The literature demonstrates the growing importance of integrating fog, cloud, and edge networks for intelligent 
task offloading. Despite advancements, challenges persist in maintaining real-time constraints and optimizing 
energy usage for critical applications like healthcare and disaster response. The Context-Aware Offloading 
Framework (CAOF) addresses these challenges by adopting a lightweight learning approach and context-driven 
offloading strategies for critical IoT data streams. This design overcomes limitations posed by complex deep-
learning algorithms in latency-sensitive environments. 
3. Methods and Materials 
 
The proposed framework, known as CAOF, includes all components that are hosted on cloud or cloudlet servers 
and operate within a client-server architecture. This section outlines the basic interface requirements of the 
proposed framework and explains how its components interact with each other. Efficient job offloading within 
fog/cloud systems is made possible by a three-layer framework that includes the sensory data-generating device, 
fog, and cloud. The framework allows for the distribution of computational tasks across fog and cloud machines.  
       Utilising Amazon Web Services (AWS) for its versatility and cost-effectiveness, the framework is designed 
to establish a middleware-based architecture that serves as a smart gateway. This gateway is designed to extract 
valuable information from sensor data, including analysing behaviour, utilising machine learning, and making 
contextual inferences. In addition, it analyses data to help with decision-making and enables applications to easily 
handle larger workloads.

6. Conclusion and Future Scope 
 
Even when utilising cutting-edge networking technologies, running delay-sensitive applications in conjunction 
with cloud services might be difficult since these programs frequently exceed crucial performance thresholds in 
areas such as latency, energy usage, bandwidth, and reaction time. This is the case even when applications make 
use of the cloud. The incorporation of a middleware layer in the architectural framework of the Internet of Things 
(IoT) presents a possible solution for addressing these challenges, while also meeting the requirement for efficient 
job offloading. This is important both for addressing these challenges and for maintaining the need for efficient 
task offloading. 
6.1. Conclusion 
 
Despite advancements in networking technologies, executing time-sensitive IoT applications alongside cloud 
services remains challenging. These applications often struggle to meet critical performance benchmarks in areas 
like latency, energy consumption, bandwidth, and response time, even within virtual private clouds (VPCs). The 
middleware layer, a fundamental component of the IoT infrastructure, emerges as a promising solution. It can 
address these limitations while facilitating efficient task offloading. 
Fog computing offers undeniable advantages for IoT applications by reducing latency and improving 
responsiveness. However, fog nodes are often limited in processing power, hindering their ability to handle 
computationally intensive tasks effectively. Therefore, fog computing is not viewed as a complete replacement 
for cloud computing, but rather as a complementary layer that leverages the strengths of both paradigms. 
The proposed framework capitalizes on this synergy. The framework facilitates optimal offloading decisions 
by strategically utilizing fog nodes for tasks suited to their capabilities and offloading demanding computations 
to the cloud. This hybrid approach optimizes resource utilization and ensures timely processing. 


  The proposed Context-Aware Offloading Framework (CAOF) leverages machine learning for intelligent 
offloading decisions within fog-cloud environments. CAOF employs machine learning classification techniques 
to analyze data and select relevant features for decision-making. Combining feature selection and classification, 
this approach acts as a learning method within the framework. CAOF utilizes a hybrid learning model based on 
logistic regression to identify optimal offloading scenarios. By analyzing contextual information associated with 
incoming data, CAOF determines the most effective course of action - processing the data locally, offloading it 
to the cloud, or utilizing other available resources. This approach aims to improve overall system performance 
and minimize energy consumption. Simulation results demonstrate the reliability of the suggested solution. An 
Amazon Web Services (AWS) environment is created, and a smart gateway is implemented in the middleware as 
a Greengrass setup. The smart gateway determines, based on the contextual information of the incoming data, 
whether it should perform computations on any of the Elastic Cloud Compute (EC2) instances or directly send 
the data to the cloud. The smart gateway performs additional analysis on the requirements of the data processing 
needs or the criticality of the information, and then, depending on the results, either sends it to a small capacity 
instance named "SM" or keeps it to itself, where the smart gateway itself can process the data as a medium capacity 
instance named as "ME" or to the large-scale instance named as "XL" machine. "SM and XL" are abbreviations 
for a small machine and a large AWS instance of machines, respectively. The CAOF selects the best available 
alternatives to ensure that performance gains in terms of time consumption, memory consumption, CPU 
utilization, and energy efficiency are achieved.  
A smart gateway framework that handles the offloading decision-making process based on data context is 
offered as a solution. The objective of this framework is to achieve effective and efficient offloading decisions by 
introducing a hybrid method. It uses various kinds of fog-based cloud environments and machine-learning 
reasoning approaches to make these inferences. Feature selection and classification are used as the learning 
methodology in this approach, which further enhances its capabilities through an ensemble approach with 
objective to provide the best offloading solution, a hybrid logistic regression-based learning is specifically 
employed for attaining the optimal offloading solution. 
 The total computation time including RTT for the healthcare IoT infrastructure that uses FC with the combination 
of IoT core cloud takes 2.82, 5.07, and 4.29 seconds from the base machine to smart gateway and gateway to ME, 
SM and XL EC2 instances respectively. On the other hand, the computation time for the ME instance is only 2.82 
seconds because the smart gateway acts as the ME instance, and there is no RTT involved from the smart gateway 
to the EC2 instance. The relative time, in seconds, that it takes to reach the Internet of Things core cloud from the 
base machine including the smart gateway is 5.41 seconds an average. CAOF offers a energy- and time-efficient 
framework while reaching an overall accuracy of approximately 80.4 percent on multiclass classification. The 
introduction of the context-aware framework and the implementation of an intelligent offloading approach are 
projected to enhance the capabilities of Internet of Things (IoT) applications. This enhancement will enable these 
applications to meet the requirements for fast response times and other critical performance characteristics. 
 
6.2. Future Scope of the Work 
This research demonstrates the potential of integrating Fog Computing (FC) within the middleware layer to 
enhance service delivery at the network edge. This approach can optimize energy efficiency and responsiveness 
for real-time applications, as exemplified by the implementation within healthcare systems. Building upon this 
foundation, several promising avenues exist for further development: 
• 
Enhancing Framework Generalizability: Future investigations can explore incorporating additional 
parameters during the design phase. This broader scope can extend the framework's applicability to real-
world software design, fostering seamless integration with mobile applications and devices. 
• 
Holistic Offloading Decisions: A crucial area for future research is expanding the factors considered 
during offloading decisions. This includes incorporating data privacy, information security, and device 
security considerations to create a more comprehensive and secure offloading strategy. 
• 
Resilient Offloading Strategy: Fault tolerance among edge devices is a vital factor for robust offloading 
decisions. Future research can investigate the implementation of intelligent data shifting mechanisms 
between edge nodes. Such mechanisms can potentially mitigate server failure scenarios and ensure 
uninterrupted offloading capabilities. 
• 
Blockchain Integration Potential: Integrating and testing blockchain-based applications within 
offloading scenarios holds significant promise. These applications typically demand high processing 
power. Exploring tailored offloading strategies specifically for blockchain applications can unlock 
substantial benefits in terms of performance and efficiency. 
• 
Next-Generation Network Integration: Future studies can investigate the seamless integration of 
CAOF with emerging 5G and 6G network infrastructures. A particular focus should be placed on the 


handoff mechanism within these networks to ensure seamless computational offloading for mobile cloud 
computing environments. 
• 
Scalability and Large-Scale Validation: While simulations were conducted on AWS EC2 testbeds 
under diverse scenarios and offloading techniques, validating the framework with thousands of devices 
in large-scale IoT networks remains a crucial direction. Future efforts should explore extensive testing 
to assess performance, resource utilization, and decision-making efficiency at scale. 
By pursuing these research directions, we can further refine and extend the capabilities of the CAOF framework, 
specifically the proposed framework lays the foundation for a context-aware offloading approach with potential 
for future integration with blockchain technology by implementing blockchain technology within the framework 
to enhance security and trust in data transmission and storage. This continuous exploration holds the potential to 
revolutionize the way we utilize offloading strategies in edge computing environments, empowering a new era of 
efficient, responsive, and secure applications.

Abstract: In the world of interconnected devices also referred to as the Internet of Things (IoT) in the modern era, it’s important to ensure that computing resources are allocated efficiently to nearby devices such as edge, fog, or cloud systems to meet resource needs. However, problems such as delays in data transmission, high energy consumption, and slow response times can negatively impact the performance of time-sensitive applications in cloud-based environments. This paper presents the Context-Aware Offloading Framework (CAOF) for resource-constrained IoT applications. CAOF leverages contextual information to identify scenarios where offloading tasks to the cloud or to the local instances are beneficial. The framework aims to make optimal offloading decisions to improve system performance and minimize energy consumption. The effectiveness of CAOF is evaluated through simulations, comparing its performance against established offloading frameworks. CAOF is implemented as a middleware solution within an Amazon Web Services (AWS) ecosystem. This middleware integrates a Greengrass intelligent gateway that dynamically determines how to handle incoming data based on contextual information. The intelligent gateway can either process the data on local Elastic Cloud Compute (EC2) instances, effectively creating a fog layer, or send it directly to the cloud for further processing. Experimental results demonstrate that CAOF achieves an energy consumption of 0.0011 joules approximately, with an memory utilization of 3.46 MB calculated as and average over all the EC2 machines. The framework execution time, averaging 4.07 seconds on edge, 5.41 seconds on cloud, and only 0.56 seconds when leveraging EC2 instances specifically, including an 80.4% accuracy in multi-class classification tasks. The CAOF systematically selects the most suitable alternatives for each offloading scenario to optimize efficiency in terms of time, memory, CPU, and energy consumption. The proposed smart gateway framework utilizes a hybrid approach to make optimal offloading decisions by considering contextual data. The research concludes with the design and development of an edge or fog-based framework that uses smart computing to make decisions using machine learning reasoning. The proposed framework architecture incorporates feature selection, classification, and hybrid logistic regression-based learning for the most effective offloading solution.
